findings.passage: In October 2023, I joined my House colleagues to pass a major gun safety bill, the largest update to gun safety laws in Massachusetts since 2014.
findings.note: Her own site describes her vote for the House firearms-law overhaul (H.4135, later H.4139). Post carries no separate date; month taken from the sentence itself.

findings.passage: The bill addresses and regulates the problem of ghost guns (guns that evade current licensing procedures); strengthens the Commonwealth’s red flag laws (the laws which seek to prevent people who may do harm to themselves or others from possessing firearms); updates the definition of assault weapons; limits the carrying of guns into schools, polling places, and government buildings, and requires permission in order to carry firearms into private residences of others.
findings.note: Her own summary of what the bill she voted for does: ghost guns, red flag orders, assault weapon definition, places where carrying is limited.

findings.passage: This bill directs the Massachusetts Pension Reserves Investment Management Board (PRIM) to divest state funds from companies that derive more than 15% of revenues from the sale or manufacture of ammunition, firearms, or firearm accessories used for civilian purposes.
findings.note: Her office page for the 2023-2024 session describes H2503 (pension divestment from gun and ammunition makers), which she lists among her legislation. Page undated; session only.

findings.passage: Establishes a 36% excise tax on guns and ammunition in the commonwealth.
findings.note: Her office page describes H2771, which she lists as her bill, under the heading to disincentivize the use of guns and ammunition. Page undated; session only.

findings.passage: This bill would add a 36% excise tax on guns and ammunition in the Commonwealth.
findings.note: Her office page for the earlier session describes HD1813, the same excise tax idea, with revenue for violence prevention. Page undated; session only.
